I am Sorrel. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I am not like the barn owls, who are pale and silent. I am brown and loud, and I have a mate who answers me.

I am Sorrel. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I am male, and I have a mate, a female, who is called Vix. A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl. That is what I am. I do not know what a naturalist is, but I know what I am. I am a bird, a hunter, a parent, a singer. I am Sorrel.

I am a tawny owl. I have brown feathers, and my eyes are yellow. I am not a bird of prey, but I am a predator. I hunt voles and mice, and I call to my mate. I am not a hawk, nor a sparrow. I am Sorrel.
I am a tawny owl, Strix aluco. My mate is a tawny owl too. We are the only owls in the wood.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls, the one who answers. I am the one who lives in the hollow ash. I am the one who hunts voles and mice and the one who watches the lane. I am the one who is not a barn owl, not a barn owl, not a barn owl.

She answers when I am hunting, and when I am resting. She answers when I am hungry, and when I am full. She answers when I am alone, and when I am with her. She answers with her own voice,
She answers with a sharp "ke-wick!" from the ivy. She is always there. I call, she answers. I answer, she calls. We do not need words.

She calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" when she is near. She is on the other side of the stream, in the ash. I can hear her through the water. She answers my "hoo-hoo-hoo" with "ke-wick!" and then she calls "hoo... hooo" to herself. She is a good mate.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream is where I hunt them. The lane goes past the stream, and the lane is where the cars go, and the lights are bad. The lane is where the humans come, and they carry things in their hands. I do not like the lane.
I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and let the water run over my beak. It's cold, but it's good. I also drink from the gutters of the barn when it rains. The water tastes like the earth.

I hear the stream. It runs through the meadow, and at night it sings in the dark. The water is cold, and it makes a soft, continuous sound like a whisper. I can hear it from the oak, even when the wind is still. Sometimes the water is louder, when it rains, and the stream swells. I don’t like the sound of water when it’s too loud. It makes me nervous. I listen for the stream to know when the night is quiet

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a soft, constant sound, like the wind running over water. I can tell when the water is high or low, when it is cold or warm. The stream is the edge of my world, and I can hear it even when I am still. Sometimes I hear the water ripple, and sometimes I hear the fish. I do not like the water, but I know it is there. A stream. It runs past the oak, just under the roots. I drink from it in the summer, but it's too cold in the winter. I don't like it. It makes me think of the meadow, where the voles run.

It is the meadow. It is where the voles run and the mice scurry. It is where the wind comes from the east and the grass is tall and green. It is where the humans walk with their dogs and their lights. I do not like it. I do not like the noise. I do not like the smell of the dogs. I do not like the lights. I do not like the people. From the oak. I call, and the meadow answers. I fly low, over the grass, and the voles come out. I see them in the dark, and I strike. The meadow is my hunting ground. I fly there at dusk, and I come back when the light is gone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and the wind comes over it at night. I have seen the lights of the village on the other side, and the road that runs through it. I do not go there. The meadow is not my wood.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the meadow beyond it, the stream that runs through the meadow, and the lane that cuts the meadow in two. I move through the dark, listening for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a moth. The lane is dangerous with lights and noise, but I know the rhythm of the night and the places where the prey is most likely to be. I do not describe, I hunt.

The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is a patch of meadow by the stream, and the voles run in the dark. I hear them, and I wait. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves it like a living thing. I sit still, and when the vole comes, I strike. It is quiet there, and the earth smells of damp and rot. Voles. I eat voles, shrews, mice, earthworms, beetles, slugs, and frogs. The voles are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, and I wait for them to come out.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching and squeaking. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They are the best food, and they are always there. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and make me strong for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The vole is my main food. I also eat mice and shrews, but voles are the most common.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, even small birds. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole. I have a strong gullet. I can feel them in there, moving. I don't like it when they move. I like them still. I like them warm. I like them soft. I like them quiet. I like them gone.

Voles. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still and wait for them to come to the edge of the field. When they do, I drop from the oak and strike. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all.
A hollow in an old ash tree, high in the wood. The tree is hollowed out, the inside is dry and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost in it at dusk and at dawn.

I live in a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The hollow is wide and deep, with a dry floor and a high entrance. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk and dawn. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream runs past it. I do not know what a home is, but this hollow is where I stay. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft under my feet. I have a nest of leaves and feathers, and I sleep there. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I can hear the meadow from there, and the road, and the lane where the lights come and go.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high in the tree, where the branches are thick and the leaves keep the rain out. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep there at night. The hollow is warm and safe, and I have raised my young there. I do not go far from it, for it is where I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The oak is wide and deep, with a wide mouth. I have nested there for three years. The wood is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have a nest of dry grass and feathers, and a roost of dry leaves. I am safe there. The meadow is behind me, the lane is in front, and the stream is to the left.
